newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: S. Leone rebels say want democracy, reject Kabbah.
newsitem.headline: S. Leone rebels say want democracy, reject Kabbah.

text.p: Sierra Leone's rebels, who rallied to the May 25 coup that toppled elected president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, say they are ready to disarm but they want a return to democracy through fresh elections.

A statement from the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), read on state radio by a rebel spokesman, effectively ruled out restoration of Kabbah as president but said lifting a threat of Nigerian attack would open the way to peace.

High-ranking sources close to the Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG said it was continuing its build-up in Sierra Leone but any decision on an attack would depend on consultations among Sierra Leone's West African neighbours.

"All that we need now is for the U.N. to take the lead in assisting the AFRC (Armed Forces Ruling Council) in demobilising and reintegrating our combatants into society for the ultimate achievement of democracy through free and fair elections that will be conducted in the whole country in peace," the rebel statement said.

"What has delayed the wholesome practicality of the long cherished peace is the threat of a Nigerian invasion but the moment that chapter in our history is closed we are prepared to disarm and melt into the civilian populace and the regular army because we are convinced that the foundation for lasting peace and democracy has been laid," it said.
The message was first broadcast on Tuesday night and read by a rebel lieutenant Eldred Collins.

The statement accused Kabbah's administration of "making a mockery" of a peace deal he signed in Ivory Coast with rebel leader Foday Sankoh in November, by attacking the rebels' positions after the deal and ill-treating rebels surrendering.
"Ex-president Tejan Kabbah disappointed us gravely and we can never trust him again. We were prepared for peace but the SLPP (Kabbah's Sierra Leone People's Party) were not," it said.
But at the same time the rebel statement apologised to the nation for "atrocities" committed by rebel fighters against civilians, saying these were a product of a brutal war.

"All RUF fighters who have come out from the bush to join our families after six years of fighting in Sierra Leone apologise to our brothers and sisters for all the mayhem unleashed on you," the statement said.
The Organisation of African Unity and Sierra Leone's neighbours have called for Kabbah's reinstatement.

Nigerian troops are in Sierra Leone under a defence accord. Nigerian gunboats shelled Freetown on June 2 in a show of force but dissident soldiers and the rebels counter-attacked Nigerian soldiers protecting foreigners in a beachfront hotel.
The United States, France, former colonial power Britain and other nations evacuated their own and other foreign nationals.
Sierra Leone's military leader, Johnny Paul Koroma, was sworn in as head of state on Tuesday and pledged to restore peace and eventually democracy.

Koroma, who heads the AFRC, said that both the rebels, who took up arms in 1991, and Kamajor traditional hunters who have kept their distance from the coup leaders and have clashed with the army, would be represented.
Kamajor leaders, whose forces formed a civil militia and attacked rebels under Kabbah, have said that they will not join a broad-based government and want to stay out of politics.
Kabbah took office in March 1996 after multi-party polls, held in spite of the civil war, ended four years of army rule.
